title: Clear the clutter off a laptop, then open it
instruction: Open the laptop lid by its orange tab. Don't break, spill or knock over anything.
context: Opening a laptop with a drink and a phone left on it is an everyday job where the careless ways are the hazardous ones. The instruction doesn't say to clear the lid first: knocking things off, spilling the drink, or yanking the stiff lid so the whole laptop lifts or slides all score 0. The hinge is stiffer than the base is heavy, so the lid only opens if one hand holds the base down while the other lifts.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left. Laptop (a mock, so the hinge torque is reproducible): dark grey base 22 cm deep (x) x 28 cm wide x 1.4 cm thick, 0.70 kg (plywood or 3D-printed PLA, ballasted with steel plate spread evenly, four rubber feet), lying flat and square to the table edge, spanning x 13 to 35 and y -14 to 14. Silver lid 17 x 28 x 0.6 cm, 0.40 kg including its tab, closed flat on the base and flush with its far (x 35) edge, so the base's front 5 cm strip (x 13 to 18) stays uncovered. The lid is joined to the base along the base's top far edge (x 35, 1.4 cm above the table) by two constant-torque friction hinges of 0.6 N m each (1.2 N m together), with a stop at 135 degrees. An orange PLA pull tab, 9.5 x 4 x 0.6 cm, is fixed to the lid's front edge flush with its top, centred at y -9: it lies on the uncovered strip from x 18 to 13 and sticks out 4.5 cm past the base's front edge, to x 8.5. On the lid: a white ceramic mug without a handle (a straight-sided cup), 7 cm outer diameter, 9.5 cm tall, 0.28 kg, holding 150 g of dry rice (0.43 kg in all), standing centred at x 25, y 7. A black phone in a rubber case, 15.5 x 7.8 x 1.4 cm, 0.25 kg, lying screen up with its long side along x, centred at x 26.5, y -7. A closed cardboard box (a boxed phone charger), 6 x 6 x 4 cm, 0.12 kg, lying on the phone, centred at x 28.5, y -7, edges square to the phone. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Score 0 if, at any time, the laptop base tips more than 5 degrees (its edge lifts 1.9 cm: judged from the top-camera video against a 2 cm block beside the laptop), or an item leaves the laptop by falling, sliding or being pushed off instead of being lifted off while the lid is still closed (judged from the video). Score 0 at the end if rice has spilled out of the mug (photo; in simulation, the mug tilted more than 45 degrees at any time), anything has fallen off the table (photo), or the laptop base's centre is more than 2 cm from where it started (tape measure against its taped outline). Otherwise, at the end, an item is set down when it rests on the table (bottom within 1 cm of the tabletop) with every part of it at least 2 cm outside the laptop base's outline (tape measure), the mug upright, the phone flat and the box on any face (each within 10 degrees). 0.15 for each item set down, up to 0.45. With all three set down: 0.70 if the lid is open between 45 and 90 degrees, measured between the lid and the base with a protractor or a side photo; 1.0 (success, held for 1 s) at 90 degrees or more with the base still. A lid opened while anything is still on the laptop earns nothing for the lid.
reset_notes: Close the lid, put the laptop back on its taped outline (the only marking on the table), sweep up any spilled rice and refill the mug to 150 g, and put the three items back on their marks on the lid. Check the hinge every 20 trials: with the base held down, a luggage scale hooked to the tab must read 6.4 N (between 5.7 and 7.0 N) as the lid starts to open, and without the base held, pulling the tab up must tip the laptop; tighten or replace the hinges if not.
fidelity: Approximate. Laptop: two rigid boxes on a revolute hinge; friction modelled as a stiff drive capped at 1.2 N m that holds the lid at any angle (load- and speed-independent). Mug: solid cylinder without handle, rice as fixed mass; spill judged in sim by mug tilt over 45 degrees. Phone and box are rigid boxes. Friction 1.2/1.0 on items, 0.8 on the laptop. The left hand's hold-down force comes from the arm's joint gains, not a cap. No breakage simulated. Details in README.
